q: The budgeted working hours of a factory are 12,000 and the actual hours worked are 10,800. The standard fixed overhead absorption rate is Rs 6 per hour. The fixed overhead capacity variance is:
e: Capacity variance = (Budgeted hours - Actual hours) x Standard rate = (12,000 - 10,800) x 6 = Rs 7,200 (Adverse), because part of the capacity remained unutilised.

q: In a factory, 75 hours were lost as idle time. The standard wage rate is Rs 48 per hour. The idle time variance is:
e: Idle time variance = Idle hours x Standard rate = 75 x 48 = Rs 3,600 (Adverse); wages paid for unproductive time are always an adverse variance.

q: The actual variable overheads incurred by a factory are Rs 96,000. The actual hours worked are 8,000 and the standard variable overhead rate is Rs 11 per hour. The variable overhead expenditure variance is:
e: Variable overhead expenditure variance = Actual overheads - (Actual hours x Standard rate) = 96,000 - (8,000 x 11) = 96,000 - 88,000 = Rs 8,000 (Adverse).

q: In variance analysis, a variance is regarded as a 'controllable' variance when:

options.A: It can be significantly influenced by the actions of the manager of the responsibility centre concerned within the period
options.B: It arises from factors wholly outside the enterprise, such as a change in the rates of taxation
options.C: It is too small in amount to be worth investigating
options.D: It recurs in every accounting period without exception

e: A variance is controllable when the manager of the responsibility centre concerned can significantly influence it by his own actions within the period; variances from external factors are uncontrollable.

q: In a process, 10,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 2,13,000. Normal loss is 5% of the input and the scrap realises Rs 8 per unit. The cost per unit of the good output is:
e: Normal loss = 5% of 10,000 = 500 units, scrap value 500 x 8 = Rs 4,000; cost per good unit = (2,13,000 - 4,000) / 9,500 = Rs 22.

q: In a process, 9,000 units were completed and transferred to the next process during a period. The closing work-in-progress is 2,400 units, which are 75% complete in respect of all cost elements. The equivalent production for the period is:
e: Equivalent production = Completed units + (Closing WIP x Degree of completion) = 9,000 + 2,400 x 75% = 9,000 + 1,800 = 10,800 units.

q: A joint cost of Rs 5,40,000 is to be apportioned between joint products A and B on the basis of their sales values at the split-off point: A — Rs 9,00,000 and B — Rs 6,00,000. The share of the joint cost borne by product A is:
e: Total split-off sales value = 9,00,000 + 6,00,000 = Rs 15,00,000; A's share of joint cost = 5,40,000 x 9,00,000 / 15,00,000 = Rs 3,24,000.

q: A joint product can be sold at the split-off point for Rs 95 per unit. It can alternatively be processed further at an additional cost of Rs 38 per unit and then sold for Rs 128 per unit. Processing the product further will result in:

options.A: A loss of Rs 5 per unit, so the product should be sold at the split-off point itself
options.B: A gain of Rs 5 per unit, so the product should be processed further
options.C: A gain of Rs 33 per unit, so the product should be processed further
options.D: Neither gain nor loss, so the firm may choose either course

e: Further processing adds revenue of 128 - 95 = Rs 33 per unit against extra cost of Rs 38, a net loss of Rs 5 per unit, so the product should be sold at the split-off point.

q: Under activity-based costing, the despatch cost pool of a plant is Rs 4,80,000 and the total number of customer orders despatched in the period is 2,400. A product which accounts for 150 despatched orders will be charged with despatch cost of:
e: Cost driver rate = 4,80,000 / 2,400 orders = Rs 200 per order; despatch cost charged to the product = 150 orders x 200 = Rs 30,000.

q:
Consider the following statements about activity-based costing:
1. Overheads are first traced to activities and are then assigned to products on the basis of cost drivers.
2. Batch-level activity costs vary in direct proportion to the number of units produced in each batch.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
e: Statement 1 is correct: ABC traces overheads to activities and assigns them by cost drivers. Statement 2 is false, because batch-level costs vary with the number of batches, not units per batch. Hence 1 only.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 8,00,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 2,60,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 5 years at 14% is 3.433. The Net Present Value of the project is:

A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 7,00,000. Its net cash inflows are Rs 3,00,000 at the end of Year 1 (present value factor at 15% = 0.870), Rs 3,00,000 at the end of Year 2 (present value factor at 15% = 0.756) and Rs 2,50,000 at the end of Year 3 (present value factor at 15% = 0.658). The Net Present Value of the project is:
The present value of Rs 6,00,000 receivable at the end of 3 years, discounted at 12% (present value factor 0.712), is:
e: Present value = Amount x PV factor = 6,00,000 x 0.712 = Rs 4,27,200.

q: Rs 80,000 invested today at 10% per annum compound interest will grow in 4 years to (the compound value factor for 4 years at 10% is 1.464):
e: Future value = Amount x Compound value factor = 80,000 x 1.464 = Rs 1,17,120.

q: A machine costing Rs 11,00,000 generates a net cash inflow of Rs 2,75,000 per year. Its payback period is:
e: Payback period = Initial cost / Annual cash inflow = 11,00,000 / 2,75,000 = 4 years.

q: A project costing Rs 9,60,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 2,40,000 in Year 1, Rs 3,60,000 in Year 2 and Rs 4,80,000 in Year 3. Its payback period is:
e: Cumulative inflows are Rs 2,40,000 (Year 1) and Rs 6,00,000 (Year 2); the balance Rs 3,60,000 comes from Year 3's Rs 4,80,000 in 9 months, so payback = 2 years 9 months.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 4,50,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 1,50,000 at the end of Year 1, Rs 2,00,000 at the end of Year 2 and Rs 2,00,000 at the end of Year 3. The discounted payback period of the project is:
e: Cumulative discounted inflows are Rs 1,50,000 (Year 1) and Rs 3,50,000 (Year 2); the balance Rs 1,00,000 is half of Year 3's Rs 2,00,000, so discounted payback = 2 years 6 months.

q: A project's Net Present Value is (+) Rs 8,000 at a discount rate of 14% and (-) Rs 8,000 at a discount rate of 18%. By interpolation, its internal rate of return is approximately:
The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 9,90,000 and its initial investment is Rs 9,00,000. The Profitability Index of the project is:
e: Profitability Index = PV of future cash inflows / Initial investment = 9,90,000 / 9,00,000 = 1.10; an index above 1 means a positive NPV.

q: An investment of Rs 9,50,000 is expected to yield an average annual profit after depreciation and tax of Rs 76,000. The Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: ARR on initial investment = Average annual profit / Initial investment x 100 = 76,000 / 9,50,000 x 100 = 8%.

q: An investment of Rs 8,50,000 has an expected salvage value of Rs 50,000 at the end of its life, so that the average investment over its life is Rs 4,50,000. If the average annual profit after depreciation and tax is Rs 63,000, the Average Rate of Return computed on the average investment is:
e: ARR = Average annual profit / Average investment x 100 = 63,000 / 4,50,000 x 100 = 14%; average investment = (8,50,000 + 50,000) / 2 = Rs 4,50,000.

q: A project has a Net Present Value of Rs 75,000 and the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the cost of capital is 2.5. Its Equivalent Annual Annuity (equivalent annual benefit) is:
e: Equivalent Annual Annuity = NPV / Annuity factor = 75,000 / 2.5 = Rs 30,000 per year.

q: A company's capital structure consists of equity capital of Rs 15,00,000 (cost 15%), preference capital of Rs 5,00,000 (cost 11%) and debt of Rs 10,00,000 (after-tax cost 8%). Its weighted average cost of capital is:
A company's capital structure consists of debt of Rs 6,00,000 with an after-tax cost of 7% and equity of Rs 14,00,000 with a cost of 16%. Its weighted average cost of capital is:
A company issues 13% debentures at par. If the tax rate is 30%, the after-tax cost of debt is:
e: After-tax cost of debt = Interest rate x (1 - Tax rate) = 13% x (1 - 0.30) = 9.1%, since interest is a tax-deductible expense.

q: A company issues 9% debentures of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 75 per debenture. Ignoring tax and redemption premium, the cost of debt is:
e: Cost of debt = Annual interest / Net proceeds = 9 / 75 = 12%; since the debentures were issued at a discount, the effective cost exceeds the 9% coupon rate.

q: A company issues 8% preference shares of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 80 per share. The cost of preference capital is:
e: Cost of preference capital = Preference dividend / Net proceeds = 8 / 80 = 10%; issuing at a discount raises the effective cost above the 8% dividend rate.

q: A company issues new equity shares at Rs 100 per share, incurring flotation costs of Rs 5 per share. The dividend expected next year is Rs 9.50 per share and dividends are expected to grow at 5% per year. The cost of the new equity capital is:
e: Cost of new equity = D1 / (Price - Flotation cost) + Growth = 9.50 / (100 - 5) + 5% = 10% + 5% = 15%.

q: A share is expected to pay a dividend of Rs 6 per share next year. Its market price is Rs 48 and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 6% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
e: Cost of equity (dividend growth model) = D1 / Market price + Growth = 6 / 48 + 6% = 12.5% + 6% = 18.5%.

q: Using the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the risk-free rate is 6%, the expected market return is 13% and the beta of the share is 1.6, the cost of equity is:
e: CAPM: Cost of equity = Risk-free rate + Beta x (Market return - Risk-free rate) = 6% + 1.6 x (13% - 6%) = 6% + 11.2% = 17.2%.

q: Under the 'residual' theory of dividend policy, a company pays dividends to its shareholders:

options.A: Only out of the earnings remaining after financing all acceptable (profitable) investment opportunities, so that the payout fluctuates with the availability of such opportunities
options.B: At a constant rate per share every year, whatever the investment needs
options.C: Equal to 100% of its earnings in every year
options.D: Only when it has no debt outstanding in its capital structure

e: Under the residual theory, dividends are a residual: earnings first finance all profitable investment opportunities and only the balance is distributed, so the payout fluctuates with investment needs.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 42,00,000, variable costs are Rs 28,00,000 and fixed costs are Rs 7,00,000. The degree of operating leverage is:
e: Contribution = 42,00,000 - 28,00,000 = Rs 14,00,000; EBIT = 14,00,000 - 7,00,000 = Rs 7,00,000; degree of operating leverage = Contribution / EBIT = 2.0.

q: An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 18,00,000 and pays interest of Rs 8,00,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = EBIT / (EBIT - Interest) = 18,00,000 / (18,00,000 - 8,00,000) = 18,00,000 / 10,00,000 = 1.8.

q: An enterprise has sales of Rs 55,00,000, variable costs of Rs 33,00,000, fixed costs of Rs 10,00,000 and interest of Rs 4,00,000. Its degree of combined leverage is:
The degree of combined leverage of an enterprise is 1.8. If its sales increase by 15%, its Earnings Per Share will increase by approximately:
e: Percentage change in EPS = Degree of combined leverage x Percentage change in sales = 1.8 x 15% = 27%.

q: A company requires total funds of Rs 10,00,000. Under Plan A it issues 1,00,000 equity shares (all-equity). Under Plan B it raises 50% of the funds by debt at 10% interest and the balance by issuing 50,000 equity shares. Ignoring tax, the indifference point (the level of EBIT at which the EPS is the same under both plans) is:
e: At the indifference point, EPS under both plans is equal: EBIT / 1,00,000 = (EBIT - 50,000 interest) / 50,000, which gives EBIT = Rs 1,00,000.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 15,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 6,00,000. Its current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities = 15,00,000 / 6,00,000 = 2.5 : 1.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 18,00,000, including stock of Rs 6,00,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 1,50,000. Current liabilities are Rs 7,00,000. The quick (acid-test) ratio is:
Long-term debt of an enterprise is Rs 13,00,000 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 10,00,000. The debt-equity ratio is:
e: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debt / Shareholders' funds = 13,00,000 / 10,00,000 = 1.3 : 1.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 45,00,000 and the cost of goods sold is Rs 27,00,000. Its gross profit ratio is:
The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 3,20,000 on sales of Rs 16,00,000. Its net profit ratio is:
e: Net profit ratio = Net profit / Sales x 100 = 3,20,000 / 16,00,000 x 100 = 20%.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 30,00,000 and its average inventory is Rs 2,00,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
e: Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of goods sold / Average inventory = 30,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 15 times.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 12,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,20,000. Taking a year of 365 days, the average collection period is:
e: Average collection period = Average debtors / Credit sales x 365 = 1,20,000 / 12,00,000 x 365 = 36.5 days.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 14,00,000 and the interest payable is Rs 2,00,000. The interest coverage ratio is:
e: Interest coverage ratio = Profit before interest and tax / Interest = 14,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 7 times.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 11,20,000 and its capital employed is Rs 28,00,000. The Return on Capital Employed is:
e: ROCE = Profit before interest and tax / Capital employed x 100 = 11,20,000 / 28,00,000 x 100 = 40%.

q: The net profit after tax of a company is Rs 8,40,000 and the preference dividend payable is Rs 90,000. If the company has 1,50,000 equity shares, its Earnings Per Share (EPS) is:
e: EPS = (Net profit after tax - Preference dividend) / Number of equity shares = (8,40,000 - 90,000) / 1,50,000 = Rs 5.00.

q: The market price of a company's share is Rs 110 and its Earnings Per Share is Rs 10. The price-earnings (P/E) ratio is:
e: P/E ratio = Market price per share / Earnings per share = 110 / 10 = 11.

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 3,60,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 48,000 and a loss of Rs 10,000 on the sale of plant, and after crediting a profit of Rs 25,000 on the sale of investments. The funds from operations are:
e: Funds from operations = 3,60,000 + Depreciation 48,000 + Loss on sale of plant 10,000 - Profit on sale of investments 25,000 = Rs 3,93,000; non-cash and non-operating items are adjusted.

q: An enterprise's operating profit before working capital changes is Rs 5,60,000. During the year, its stock increased by Rs 50,000, its debtors increased by Rs 20,000 and its creditors decreased by Rs 15,000. The cash from operations is:
e: Cash from operations = 5,60,000 - Increase in stock 50,000 - Increase in debtors 20,000 - Decrease in creditors 15,000 = Rs 4,75,000; rises in current assets and falls in current liabilities absorb cash.

q: During a year, the current assets of an enterprise increased by Rs 1,80,000 and its current liabilities increased by Rs 2,40,000. The net change in its working capital is:
e: Change in working capital = Increase in current assets - Increase in current liabilities = 1,80,000 - 2,40,000, i.e. a decrease of Rs 60,000.

q: In preparing a cash flow statement under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), the acquisition of machinery by a company by issuing shares to the vendor is:

options.A: A non-cash transaction, which is excluded from the cash flow statement (being disclosed elsewhere), since no cash moves in the transaction
options.B: Shown as an investing outflow and a financing inflow, at the value of the machinery
options.C: Shown as an operating activity of the company
options.D: Shown partly as an operating activity and partly as an investing activity

e: Under AS-3, acquiring machinery against issue of shares involves no movement of cash; such non-cash investing and financing transactions are excluded from the cash flow statement and disclosed elsewhere.

q: The net earnings of a railway are Rs 13,600 crore and its capital-at-charge is Rs 1,70,000 crore. The return on capital-at-charge is:
e: Return on capital-at-charge = Net earnings / Capital-at-charge x 100 = 13,600 / 1,70,000 x 100 = 8%.

q: A railway earned gross traffic receipts of Rs 3,50,000 crore against ordinary working expenses of Rs 3,29,000 crore. Its Operating Ratio is:
e: Operating Ratio = Ordinary working expenses / Gross traffic receipts x 100 = 3,29,000 / 3,50,000 x 100 = 94%.

q: The Operating Ratio of a railway is 90% and its gross traffic receipts are Rs 4,50,000 crore. Its ordinary working expenses are:
e: Ordinary working expenses = Operating Ratio x Gross traffic receipts = 90% of 4,50,000 = Rs 4,05,000 crore.

q: A proposed railway work is estimated to cost Rs 900 crore and is expected to yield net annual earnings of Rs 99 crore after meeting the additional working expenses. The anticipated rate of return on the work, and its financial status, are:

options.C: 10%; the work just meets the prescribed test
options.D: 11%; the work is remunerative, as it exceeds the prescribed 10% test of remunerativeness

e: Rate of return = 99 / 900 x 100 = 11%, which exceeds the prescribed 10% test of remunerativeness, so the work is financially remunerative.

q: Budgeted sales of a product are 38,000 units. The opening stock of finished goods is 3,500 units and the closing stock is to be 5,500 units. The production budget should provide for production of:
e: Production = Budgeted sales + Closing stock - Opening stock = 38,000 + 5,500 - 3,500 = 40,000 units.

q: Production of 26,000 units is budgeted, each unit requiring 4 kg of material. The opening stock of material is 9,000 kg and the closing stock is to be 12,000 kg. The quantity of material to be purchased is:
e: Material required = 26,000 x 4 = 1,04,000 kg; purchases = 1,04,000 + Closing stock 12,000 - Opening stock 9,000 = 1,07,000 kg.

q: A cash budget for a month shows an opening cash balance of Rs 30,000, estimated receipts of Rs 2,20,000 and estimated payments of Rs 2,90,000. The enterprise must maintain a minimum cash balance of Rs 20,000 at the end of the month. The amount it will need to borrow during the month is:
e: Closing balance before borrowing = 30,000 + 2,20,000 - 2,90,000 = (-) Rs 40,000; to end the month with the minimum Rs 20,000, borrowing of Rs 60,000 is needed.

q: An enterprise pays its suppliers 30% of the purchase value in the month of purchase and the remaining 70% in the following month. Purchases were Rs 2,00,000 in the previous month and are budgeted at Rs 2,60,000 in the current month. The cash payment for purchases in the current month will be:
e: Payment = 70% of previous month's purchases + 30% of current month's purchases = 1,40,000 + 78,000 = Rs 2,18,000.

q: A budget provides for fixed costs of Rs 4,20,000 and variable costs of Rs 25 per unit. The total flexed budget allowance for an actual output of 12,000 units is:
e: Flexed budget = Fixed costs + (Variable cost per unit x Actual output) = 4,20,000 + 25 x 12,000 = Rs 7,20,000; fixed costs remain unchanged on flexing.

q: In budgetary control, the budgeted hours of a department are 12,500 and the actual hours worked are 11,250. The capacity ratio of the department is:
e: Capacity ratio = Actual hours worked / Budgeted hours x 100 = 11,250 / 12,500 x 100 = 90%.

q: A budget is best defined as:

options.A: A quantitative statement of a plan of action for a future period, expressed usually in monetary terms, prepared in advance to guide and coordinate the activities of the enterprise
options.B: A record of the actual income and expenditure of the enterprise for the past year
options.C: A statement of the assets and liabilities of the enterprise on a particular date
options.D: A forecast of the profits which the enterprise is certain to earn in the future

e: A budget is a quantitative statement of a plan of action for a future period, usually in monetary terms, prepared in advance to guide and coordinate the activities of the enterprise.

q: In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are held for 42 days, the production process takes 16 days, finished goods are held for 22 days and debtors take 48 days to pay. Suppliers allow 32 days' credit. The length of the operating cycle is:
e: Operating cycle = 42 + 16 + 22 + 48 - Suppliers' credit 32 = 96 days; the credit allowed by suppliers shortens the net cycle.

q: The annual operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 38,40,000 (reckoning a year of 360 days). Its operating cycle is 48 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
e: Working capital = Annual operating cost x (Operating cycle / 360) = 38,40,000 x 48/360 = Rs 5,12,000.

q: An enterprise has an inventory conversion period of 72 days, a receivables collection period of 42 days and a payables deferral period of 38 days. Its cash conversion cycle is:
e: Cash conversion cycle = Inventory period + Receivables period - Payables period = 72 + 42 - 38 = 76 days.

q: The current assets of an enterprise are Rs 18,00,000 and its current ratio is 3 : 1. Its net working capital is:
e: Current liabilities = 18,00,000 / 3 = Rs 6,00,000; net working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities = 18,00,000 - 6,00,000 = Rs 12,00,000.

q: Under the Tandon Committee's Method III of lending, the core (permanent) current assets are not financed by the bank at all, and the bank finances 75% of the remaining current assets after providing for current liabilities other than bank borrowings. For a borrower with total current assets of Rs 40,00,000, including core current assets of Rs 10,00,000, and current liabilities (other than bank borrowings) of Rs 6,00,000, the maximum permissible bank finance is:
e: Method III: MPBF = 75% of (Total current assets - Core current assets) - Current liabilities = 75% of 30,00,000 - 6,00,000 = 22,50,000 - 6,00,000 = Rs 16,50,000; core assets get no bank finance.

q: The projected sales of an enterprise for the coming year are Rs 75,00,000 and, on the percentage-of-sales method, its working capital is estimated at 20% of sales. The working capital requirement of the enterprise is:
e: Working capital = 20% of projected sales = 20% of 75,00,000 = Rs 15,00,000.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 750 units per week and the maximum re-order period is 6 weeks. The re-order level for the material is:
e: Re-order level = Maximum consumption x Maximum re-order period = 750 x 6 = 4,500 units.

q: The re-order level of a material is 6,300 units. Normal consumption is 450 units per week and the normal re-order period is 9 weeks. The minimum stock level is:
e: Minimum stock level = Re-order level - (Normal consumption x Normal period) = 6,300 - (450 x 9) = 6,300 - 4,050 = 2,250 units.

q: The re-order level of a material is 2,400 units and the re-order quantity is 1,700 units. Minimum consumption is 120 units per week and the minimum re-order period is 6 weeks. The maximum stock level is:
e: Maximum stock level = Re-order level + Re-order quantity - (Minimum consumption x Minimum period) = 2,400 + 1,700 - (120 x 6) = 4,100 - 720 = 3,380 units.

q: The minimum stock level of a material is 2,200 units and the re-order quantity is 2,800 units. The average stock level is:
e: Average stock level = Minimum level + Half of re-order quantity = 2,200 + 2,800/2 = 3,600 units.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 700 units per week, the normal consumption is 450 units per week and the maximum lead time is 6 weeks. The safety stock, computed as (Maximum consumption - Normal consumption) x Maximum lead time, is:
e: Safety stock = (Maximum consumption - Normal consumption) x Maximum lead time = (700 - 450) x 6 = 1,500 units.

q: The average (normal) consumption of a material is 250 units per week and the maximum re-order period for emergency purchases is 3 weeks. The danger level of the material is:
e: Danger level = Average consumption x Maximum re-order period for emergency purchases = 250 x 3 = 750 units; at this level emergency action is taken to avoid a stock-out.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 14,450 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 100 and the carrying cost is Rs 4 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:
In ABC analysis of inventory, the 'C' category items are those which:

options.A: Are few in number but account for the largest share of the annual consumption value
options.B: Constitute the bulk of the total number of items (about 70 per cent) but account for only a small share (about 10 per cent) of the total annual consumption value, and are therefore controlled by simple, loose methods
options.C: Are of medium value and need moderate control at all times
options.D: Are classified according to their physical size and weight

e: 'C' category items form the bulk of item numbers (about 70%) but only about 10% of annual consumption value, so they are controlled by simple, loose methods; 'A' items get the tightest control.

q: The annual credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 27,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,50,000. Taking a year of 360 days, the average collection period is:
e: Average collection period = Average debtors / Credit sales x 360 = 1,50,000 / 27,00,000 x 360 = 20 days.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 20,40,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,20,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:
e: Debtors turnover ratio = Credit sales / Average debtors = 20,40,000 / 1,20,000 = 17 times.

q: Annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 43,20,000 and its average creditors are Rs 2,40,000. Taking a year of 360 days, the average payment period is:
e: Average payment period = Average creditors / Credit purchases x 360 = 2,40,000 / 43,20,000 x 360 = 20 days.

q: Annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 24,00,000 and its average creditors are Rs 1,60,000. The creditors turnover ratio is:
e: Creditors turnover ratio = Credit purchases / Average creditors = 24,00,000 / 1,60,000 = 15 times.

q: A supplier offers credit terms of 3/10, net 30. The approximate annual cost of not taking the cash discount (on a 360-day year basis) is:
e: Cost of not taking the discount = [3 / (100 - 3)] x [360 / (30 - 10)] = 3/97 x 18 = 55.7% per annum.

q: Under the Baumol model of cash management, an enterprise's annual cash requirement is Rs 30,25,000, the cost of converting marketable securities into cash is Rs 40 per transaction and the opportunity interest rate is 8% per annum. The optimum cash balance, sqrt(2AT/i), is:
e: Optimum cash balance = sqrt(2 x 30,25,000 x 40 / 0.08) = sqrt(3,02,50,00,000) = Rs 55,000.

q: Under the Miller-Orr model of cash management, an enterprise fixes a lower control limit of Rs 60,000 and a spread of Rs 90,000 between the control limits. The return point (target cash balance) is:
e: Return point = Lower limit + One-third of the spread = 60,000 + 90,000/3 = Rs 90,000; the upper control limit is 60,000 + 90,000 = Rs 1,50,000.

q: Under the cash credit system of bank lending, widely used for working capital finance in India:

options.A: Interest is charged on the entire amount of the limit sanctioned, whether it is drawn or not
options.B: Interest is charged only on the amount actually drawn, that is, on the daily balance outstanding, and not on the whole limit sanctioned
options.C: The borrower must repay the entire amount outstanding at the end of every month
options.D: No security of stocks or book debts is required from the borrower

e: Under the cash credit system, interest is charged only on the amount actually drawn, that is, on the daily balance outstanding, and not on the whole limit sanctioned.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 9,80,000 on capital employed of Rs 70,00,000. The Return on Investment of the division is:
e: ROI = Profit / Capital employed x 100 = 9,80,000 / 70,00,000 x 100 = 14%.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 19,20,000 on capital employed of Rs 1,20,00,000. The cost of capital is 11%. The Residual Income of the division is:
e: Residual Income = Profit - (Cost of capital x Capital employed) = 19,20,000 - 11% of 1,20,00,000 = 19,20,000 - 13,20,000 = Rs 6,00,000.

q: The Net Operating Profit After Tax (NOPAT) of a division is Rs 27,00,000, its capital employed is Rs 1,80,00,000 and the cost of capital is 12%. Its Economic Value Added (EVA) is:
e: EVA = NOPAT - (Cost of capital x Capital employed) = 27,00,000 - 12% of 1,80,00,000 = 27,00,000 - 21,60,000 = Rs 5,40,000.

q: A selling division produces a component at a total cost of Rs 120 per unit. Under the cost-plus method of transfer pricing, with a mark-up of 25% on cost, the transfer price of the component will be:
e: Cost-plus transfer price = Total cost + 25% mark-up = 120 + 30 = Rs 150 per unit.

q: Under the two-part (two-tariff) system of transfer pricing:

options.A: Two different prices are charged to outside customers for the same product
options.B: The transfer price is revised twice a year by the head office
options.C: The buying division pays the variable cost per unit for the units transferred, plus a periodic lump-sum fixed charge covering the fixed costs and an element of profit of the selling division
options.D: The selling division is credited at the market price while the buying division is debited at cost

e: Under the two-part tariff, the buying division pays the variable cost per unit transferred plus a periodic lump-sum fixed charge covering the selling division's fixed costs and an element of its profit.

q: If the Economic Value Added (EVA) of an enterprise for a year is positive, it means that the enterprise has:

options.A: Earned a return in excess of its cost of capital and has thereby created value for its shareholders during the year
options.B: Earned a profit before tax during the year
options.C: Seen a fall in the market value of its shares during the year
options.D: No borrowed capital in its capital structure

e: Positive EVA means NOPAT exceeds the full capital charge (cost of capital x capital employed), so the enterprise earned a return above its cost of capital and created value for shareholders.

q: The expected market price of a product is Rs 2,500 per unit and the firm desires a profit margin of 20% on the selling price. The target cost of the product is:
e: Target cost = Expected price - Desired margin = 2,500 - 20% of 2,500 = 2,500 - 500 = Rs 2,000.

q: The actual cost of a product in the previous period was Rs 600 per unit. Under kaizen costing, a cost-reduction target of 8% is set for the current period. The kaizen target cost for the current period is:
e: Kaizen target cost = Previous cost less the cost-reduction target = 600 - 8% of 600 = 600 - 48 = Rs 552.

q: 'Internal benchmarking', as a technique of performance improvement, involves:

options.A: Comparing the performance of the enterprise with that of its strongest competitor
options.B: Comparing the current performance of the enterprise with its own performance in the previous year
options.C: Comparing the processes and performance of one unit, plant or branch of an organisation with those of another unit of the same organisation which performs the same function best, so that the best internal practice is adopted elsewhere
options.D: Comparing the products of the enterprise with those of the best firm in an entirely different industry

e: Internal benchmarking compares one unit, plant or branch of an organisation with another unit of the same organisation that performs the function best, so that the best internal practice is adopted elsewhere.

q: In backflush costing, the stage in the production or sales process at which the product costs are applied (flushed back) to the units produced, using predetermined rates, is known as the:
e: In backflush costing, product costs are flushed back to the units produced at predetermined rates when a trigger point, usually completion or sale of the product, is reached.

q: Value engineering was first developed by:

options.A: Frederick W. Taylor in the early years of the twentieth century
options.D: Lawrence D. Miles at the General Electric Company in the USA during the Second World War

e: Value engineering was developed by Lawrence D. Miles at the General Electric Company in the USA during the Second World War, when wartime shortages forced a search for substitutes without loss of function.

q: The sales of a factory for a period are Rs 15,00,000 and the totally variable costs (direct materials) are Rs 6,00,000. All other factory costs are treated as operating expenses. The throughput for the period is:
e: Throughput = Sales - Totally variable costs = 15,00,000 - 6,00,000 = Rs 9,00,000.

q: A factory makes two products on a bottleneck machine. Product A gives a throughput of Rs 600 per unit and takes 0.75 hour of the bottleneck machine per unit. Product B gives a throughput of Rs 500 per unit and takes 0.5 hour of the bottleneck machine per unit. To maximise the total throughput, production priority should be given to:

options.A: Product A, because its throughput per unit is higher
options.B: Both products equally, in proportion to their sales demand
options.C: Product B, because its throughput per bottleneck hour (Rs 1,000) is higher than that of Product A (Rs 800)
options.D: Product A, because it occupies the bottleneck machine for a longer time per unit

e: Throughput per bottleneck hour: A = 600 / 0.75 = Rs 800; B = 500 / 0.5 = Rs 1,000; B earns more per scarce bottleneck hour, so production priority goes to Product B.

q: An asset was purchased for Rs 6,00,000 when the general price index stood at 150. At the balance sheet date the index stands at 210. Under the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method, the restated value of the asset is:
e: CPP restatement = Historical cost x (Current index / Index at purchase) = 6,00,000 x 210/150 = Rs 8,40,000.

q: In Current Cost Accounting (CCA), 'backlog depreciation' refers to:

options.A: The depreciation charged on assets which have become obsolete
options.B: The depreciation written back in the earlier years on the historical cost of the assets
options.C: The arrears of depreciation payable by the enterprise on its assets
options.D: The shortfall in the accumulated depreciation provision which arises when fixed assets are restated at their current replacement cost, the depreciation provided in the past on historical cost being inadequate to cover the charge on the restated value

e: Backlog depreciation is the shortfall in accumulated depreciation that arises when assets are restated at current replacement cost, because depreciation provided earlier on historical cost is inadequate for the restated value.

q: In Current Cost Accounting (CCA), the various current cost adjustments (for depreciation, cost of sales and monetary working capital) are accumulated and shown in the balance sheet as part of:

options.A: The general reserve of the company
options.B: The current cost reserve, representing the amount needed to maintain the operating assets of the enterprise at their current values
options.C: The profit and loss account, as income of the year
options.D: The share capital of the company

e: In CCA, the depreciation, cost of sales and monetary working capital adjustments are accumulated in the current cost reserve, representing the amount needed to maintain the operating assets at their current values.
